lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: This is Dimension Hop. Two hosts, two realities.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Zero preparation.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: You're listening to Dimension Hop!

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: She said that before I pressed the button.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Dimension Hop. If you can hear both of us, your radio's working. If you hear three, call us.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Dimension Hop! Rolling to you live, from four seconds from now!

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: That's Dimension Hop. More from both of our realities, after this.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Mine's better. You'll see. Well, I've seen. You'll see in a bit.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: She's not wrong. I've seen her side. The sandwiches are incredible.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Quick reminder, everyone. If you can hear me before you hear Jace, your radio's working. If you hear Jace before me, check your radio. If you can hear yourself, call us, we'd love to talk to you.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: We're going to take a quick break.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: I'm already back.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: She's already back. Stay with us.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: You'll like what happens next. I did.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Welcome back to Dimension Hop, the show where two people from two different realities talk about it. I'm Jace.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: And I'm Mara, coming to you from a reality where this microphone is upside down, and so am I, and so, frankly, is my coffee.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: How do you drink it?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Carefully, Jace. From underneath.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Okay. So, Mara, I wanted to ask you. In your reality, how do people get places?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: We roll. Mostly downhill. Uphill is for emergencies.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: See, here, we just walk. With legs.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: With your legs? Both of them? At the same time?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: No, one after the other.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: That's so brave.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: It's not brave, it's walking. Babies do it.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: You make the babies do it? Jace.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Nobody makes them. They just sort of figure it out. They fall over a lot at first.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: And then they stop falling over?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Mostly.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Mostly. So your whole reality is people who are mostly not falling over. That explains a lot about your music.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: What happens if you need to go uphill, and it's not an emergency?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Then you live there now. That's just the rules.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Okay. We're going to take a quick break.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Don't go anywhere. Or do. Roll, if you have to.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Welcome back to Dimension Hop. Mara, I think something's wrong with the line. I can hear you before you talk.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Oh, yeah. That's the time zone. I'm about four seconds ahead of you.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: That's not how time zones work.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: It's how mine works. Your next question's about breakfast.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: What do you guys eat for breakfast?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: See? Anyway. We eat the evening before. It saves time.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: That doesn't—

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Yes it does, Jace. You were going to say that.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: So what's it like? Being four seconds ahead?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Honestly? Lonely. I laugh at every joke before it's told, so people think I'm laughing at them.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: I'm sorry.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: I know. You said that four seconds ago.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Is there anything good about it?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Oh, loads. I always know when the phone's about to ring. Like, now.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Who is it?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: It's me, from four seconds ago. She's fine. Don't answer it, she'll only want to talk about breakfast.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: We'll be right back.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: You already are.

clips.title: Listener Mail: Murray, Priya and the Same Letter

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: It's time for listener mail! Jace, read the first one.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: This one's from Murray, who writes: Dear Dimension Hop. In my reality, the dogs own the people. Is that normal?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Totally normal. In mine, the dogs own the dogs. It's a whole pyramid thing.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Murray goes on. My dog says I'm a good boy, but I don't think he means it.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Murray. He means it. Dogs can't lie. That's why they never run for office.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Next. From Priya, in the Damp Dimension. She writes: Dear Dimension Hop, what's the sun like?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: You take this one, Jace. We don't really have one. It's more of a rumor.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: It's warm. It's very bright. You can't look straight at it.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: So it's shy.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: No. Sort of. It comes up every single morning.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Every morning? It must be exhausted.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: I've honestly never thought about that.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Somebody should.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Last letter. From someone who signs it, The Same Letter. It says: Dear Dimension Hop. This is the same letter.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Oh, that's the same letter.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Mara, it's a different letter.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Is it, Jace? Is it?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: We're out of time.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: We're always out of time. Some of us are just further out than others. Bye, Murray!

clips.title: Listener Mail: A Letter from a Shadow

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Listener mail. And Mara, this one's unusual. The envelope's empty.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Hold it up to the light.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Oh. Oh, there's a shape on it. It's somebody lying across the paper.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: That's a letter from a shadow, Jace. That's how they write. You read the shape.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: How do you read a shape?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: With your feelings. Go on.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Okay. It's a man, sort of sitting, with his knees up. And there's a wave, along the bottom. I think he's at the sea.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: That's Greg.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Who's Greg?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Greg's the shadow that left that man, Hollis. It's been on the news. It's been on every station, Jace, where have you been?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: On this station. With you.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Fair. So what's Greg saying?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: I think he's saying, I'm okay. I think he's saying, I always wanted to see the sea, and Hollis never went anywhere, so I went.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: In my reality, shadows roll alongside you. They're like a friend whose face you never quite see. When one goes off on its own, we say it's gone to find its edges.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: That's lovely.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: It's a bit sad too. But mostly lovely.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Greg, if you're listening, send this to Hollis. Not to us. He'd love it.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: He'll know your shape, Greg. People always know the shape.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Mara, tonight I want to talk about breakfast.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: You already did, four seconds from now. Go on, though, I liked it.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: So in my reality, a lot of people have cereal.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: What's cereal?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: It's little crunchy pieces of grain, in a box. You pour them into a bowl, and then you pour milk on them.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: To make them soft.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: So you buy them crunchy, so that you can make them soft.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Yes. But not too soft. You have to eat them before they get too soft.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Oh, so it's a race.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: It's not a race.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Jace. You're racing milk. Every morning. Against your own breakfast. And you're losing.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: I'm not losing.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Have you ever got to the bottom of a bowl of cereal and found it still crunchy?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: You've never won, Jace. Not once. Not in your whole life.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Fine. What do you have for breakfast, then?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: The evening before. We eat yesterday's dinner, backwards, so it tastes like it's getting fresher. By the end, it's a shopping list.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: That's not—

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: It is.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Okay, Mara. Tonight, I'm going to explain sleep.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Oh, I love this. Go.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: So, every night, we get into bed, we lie down, we close our eyes, and for about eight hours, we're just not here.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Where are you?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Asleep.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Yes, but where?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Nowhere. Here. In the bed. But our brains go off and have dreams. You see things. Sometimes you're back at school. Sometimes you're late for something and you can't find your shoes.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: And this is supposed to be restful.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: It is restful.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Jace, every night you lie down in the dark, on purpose, for a third of your life, and your brain goes off without you to look for your shoes. And you all just agree that's fine.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: When you put it like that.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Who's guarding you?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Nobody. We lock the door.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: You lock the door, and then you leave your body in the room, alone, with your brain out, and you call it a night.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: What do you do, then?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: We roll a bit slower after dark. And we hold hands with whoever's nearest, so nobody drifts off on their own. In the morning, you say thank you. Sometimes you've never met them.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: That's actually really nice.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Yours is nice too. Weird, but nice. Sweet dreams about your shoes, Jace.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: It's time for Normal, or Not Normal! The game where Jace describes something from his reality, and I decide if it's normal.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Okay. Number one. Elevators.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Describe.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: It's a little room. You get in, the doors close, and it takes you up or down, to another floor.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: With strangers?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Sometimes, yeah.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: And what do you all do, in the little room, with the strangers?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Nothing. We face the doors. We don't talk. We watch the numbers go up.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: In silence.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Mostly. Sometimes there's music.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Jace, that's a ritual. That's a ceremony. You're all standing together, facing the same way, watching numbers, with music. Not normal.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Number two. Umbrellas. When it rains, you hold a little roof over your head, on a stick.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Oh, that's normal. We do that. We just hold it underneath.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Why underneath?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: The rain goes up here, Jace. Keep up.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Number three. Shaking hands. When you meet someone, you hold their hand, and move it up and down.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: How many times?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Two. Maybe three.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: And who decides when it stops?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Nobody knows.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Not normal. Terrifying. That's two not normals and one normal. Better luck next time, Jace's entire reality.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Mara, people keep writing in to ask about rolling. How does it actually work, day to day?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Oh, it's very simple. You tuck in, you lean, and off you go. Downhill is free. Flat is fine. Uphill is for emergencies.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: And if it's not an emergency?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Then you live there now. My aunt went up a hill once because she thought she'd left the oven on. That was nineteen years ago. She's got a lovely house up there. The oven was off.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Can't she just roll back down?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Jace, you can't roll down a hill you rolled up in a panic. Everyone would know.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: What are the other rules?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: You give way to anyone rolling with shopping. You never roll in a straight line past a bakery, it's showing off. And if you meet someone rolling the other way, you both stop, and say, after you.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: And then who goes?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Nobody, Jace. That's why there's a deer on Interstate Zero.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Do you think I could roll?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Try it. Tuck your chin in. Lean forward.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Okay. Okay, here goes.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: How was that?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: I've hit the desk. I'm under the desk now.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Then you live there now, Jace.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: That's not uphill!

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: It's not about the hill, Jace. It's about the commitment.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Mara, tonight, money. In my reality, we use money to buy things.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: What's money?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: It's little pieces of paper, and some metal circles. You give them to people, and they give you things.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Is the paper special?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Not really. It's just paper. With pictures on.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: So why do people take it?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Because everybody agrees it's worth something.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: That's it? Everybody just agrees?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Yeah. And as long as everyone keeps agreeing, it works.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Jace, that's the most romantic thing I've ever heard.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: It's not romantic, it's money.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Your whole reality runs on everybody quietly agreeing to believe in the same little bits of paper, at the same time, every single day. Nobody's checking. Everybody's just trusting each other. That's beautiful.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: I mean, sometimes it goes wrong.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Of course it does. That's how you know it's love.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: What do you use, then?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Compliments. A loaf of bread is two compliments, but they have to be about the baker's hair.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: What if the baker's bald?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Then it's about the shine, Jace. Honestly. Have you ever even bought bread?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Listener mail! Jace, there's one here in very careful handwriting.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: It's from Bev. She writes: Dear Dimension Hop. Is this the request line?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Oh, Bev.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: She goes on. I have been trying to hear a song for eleven years. It goes dum, dum, da dum, and then a man cries. I have tried the news, the sports, the advice lady, and a man selling holes. Nobody has played it. Yours sincerely, Bev.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Jace, we should play it.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: We don't have it. Nobody has it. I'm not sure it exists.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Then we'll make it. Go on. Dum, dum, da dum.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: I'm not doing that.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Jace. Bev has been looking for eleven years.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Fine. Dum. Dum. Da dum.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: And then a man cries.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: I'm not going to cry.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: You're going to cry in about four seconds, Jace.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Why is it so sad? It's three notes.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: It's the space after the third one. That's where the man is.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Bev, I hope that was close.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: It was close, Bev. I heard it first.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Mara, I've got a question. The rift. The glowing crack down the middle of the studio.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: My favorite crack.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Can we pass things through it?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Let's find out. Here, have a biscuit.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Okay, it's come through. It's upside down.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Well, it was the right way up when it left.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: No, I mean it's stuck to the ceiling.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Oh, sorry, I gave you one of ours. You'll have to eat it from underneath.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Okay, my turn. Here's a pen.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Ooh. Jace, it's arrived, but it's arrived four seconds before you sent it.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: So where is it now?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: It's in both places, and they're both a bit embarrassed. Let's not do pens.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Can I put my hand through?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Absolutely not. Well. Maybe. Do you want to?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Kind of.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Okay, but if your hand comes back holding a different coffee, that's not my fault.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Mara. I'm holding a different coffee.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Is it nice?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: It's really nice, actually.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: That's mine. Give it back.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Okay, Mara. In my reality, once a year, we celebrate the day we were born.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Because it's the day you arrived. We have cake, and candles, and everyone sings to you.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Every year?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Every year.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: But you've already arrived. You're here. We can see you. Why do you keep celebrating it?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Because it's nice to be glad someone's here.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Okay. That's actually nice. What about the candles?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: You put one candle on the cake for every year you've been alive, you make a wish, and you blow them all out.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Hang on. So the older you get, the more fire there is on the cake.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: I guess so.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: So at the end, when you're very old, it's just a cake that's on fire, and everybody stands around it, singing.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: It's not, okay, it's a little bit like that.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: We celebrate the day you leave a room. Any room. Once a year, you pick a door, and you walk out of it, and everybody cheers, and someone shouts, look at them go!

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Because you never know which door is the important one, Jace. So we cheer all of them.

clips.title: Normal or Not Normal: Small Talk

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Normal, or Not Normal, round two! Jace, your reality's been losing. Bring me something good.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Okay. Talking about the weather. When you meet someone and you don't know what to say, you say, nice day, isn't it? And they say, yes, lovely.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Even if it isn't a nice day?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Especially then. Then you say, bit grim today, isn't it? And they say, isn't it.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: So you're not really talking about the weather.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: No. You're just saying, I see you, we're both here, and we're both in this weather.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Normal. Very normal. That's the most normal thing you've ever told me. Point to Jace.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Number two. Pockets. Little bags sewn into your clothes, where you keep things.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Normal, as long as you don't check them. Do you check them?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Constantly. I pat them, to make sure my keys are still there. Every few minutes.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Not normal. Those keys aren't going anywhere, Jace. Have some faith.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Number three. Waving at boats. When a boat goes past, you wave at the people on it, and they wave back. And you'll never see them again.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Normal. Beautiful. Two points to Jace's reality. You're catching up.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Mara, we've had a lot of letters lately asking for advice.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: We're very wise.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: We are not.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: I'm a bit wise. I'm four seconds wise.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Okay. This one says: My upstairs neighbor practices the tuba at midnight. What should I do?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Move upstairs.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: That's above the neighbor.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Exactly. Then you're the upstairs neighbor. You hold all the power. Get a tuba.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: That's terrible advice. Next one. My best friend has started living four seconds in the future, and I can't keep up.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Oh, that's easy. Start your sentences early. Talk to the space where she's going to be.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: That's actually reasonable.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: I'm always reasonable four seconds from now. Next.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: My shadow left me, and I don't know how to be on my own.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Jace, this one's above our pay grade.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: We don't get paid.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Exactly. Hollis, love, call Grenda. Ninety seven point eight. She's good with shadows.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: She's good with everything.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: She's the only person I know who's never once been surprised by me.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Mara, do you have any pets?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: I have a hill.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: A pet hill.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: His name is Gerald. He's a lovely hill. Very gentle slope.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: How do you walk a hill?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: You don't walk him, Jace. He walks you. Well, you roll down him, and that counts.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Does he do tricks?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: He sits.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: Hills always sit.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Yes, but he does it when I ask.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: What does he eat?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Weather. Mostly rain. He gets a bit muddy, and then I have to brush him, which takes a weekend.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: And does he love you?

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: He lets me sit on top of him to watch the sunset, and he has never once rolled me off. If that's not love, Jace, I don't know what is.

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: I had a goldfish, when I was a kid.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: What did it do?

lines.speaker: Jace
lines.text: It went round.

lines.speaker: Mara
lines.text: Oh, Jace. Did it ever get there?
